angle: follow one release of one containerized service: the image goes into a Regional ECR repository (1), a task definition names its containers and two roles with different jobs (2), Fargate gives each task its own isolated compute (3), awsvpc gives each task its own network interface and decides how the image is pulled (4), an ECS service keeps the desired count across Availability Zones and rolls out new revisions (5), service auto scaling changes the task count while capacity providers bring the compute, Fargate Spot included (6); then the same containers under Kubernetes: EKS runs the control plane and you choose where pods run (7). On-premises options (ECS Anywhere, EKS Anywhere, EKS Distro) are recognise-only service cards in 2-services.md.

traps.belief: The task execution role gives the application in the container its permissions, for example to read an S3 bucket.
traps.truth: The task execution role is for the ECS container and Fargate agents, and its permissions are not directly accessible by the containers; the application uses the task role.

traps.belief: Fargate runs any container that EC2 capacity runs, including privileged containers, GPU work and one daemon task on every host.
traps.truth: Privileged containers are unavailable on Fargate, GPU workloads are not supported there, and Fargate does not support the DAEMON scheduling strategy.

traps.belief: When Fargate Spot capacity is not available, ECS starts the tasks on regular Fargate instead.
traps.truth: Fargate does not replace Spot capacity with on-demand capacity; a capacity provider strategy with a base on FARGATE keeps a minimum running.

traps.belief: One ECR repository in one Region serves tasks in every Region at no extra cost.
traps.truth: ECR is a Regional service; pulls from another Region add latency and data transfer costs, and replication copies images to other Regions.

traps.belief: Files that a task writes to its own storage are still there for the task that replaces it.
traps.truth: Fargate ephemeral storage is erased when the workload stops, and an EBS volume of a service task is deleted at task termination; shared, lasting files go to Amazon EFS.

traps.belief: A target group of type instance works for Fargate tasks, as it does for EC2 instances.
traps.truth: Tasks in awsvpc mode are associated with a network interface, not an instance, so the target type must be ip.

traps.belief: ECS service auto scaling also adds and removes the EC2 instances of the cluster.
traps.truth: Service auto scaling changes the desired number of tasks; EC2 instances follow only through cluster auto scaling, the managed scaling of an Auto Scaling group capacity provider.

faq.question: Can a task on AWS Fargate use a GPU?
faq.answer: No. GPU work is [not supported on AWS Fargate today] (fargate-faq-gpu-not-supported); use Amazon EC2.
faq.quote: Use Amazon EC2 for GPU workloads, which are not supported on AWS Fargate today.

faq.question: Can a workload on Fargate keep data after it stops?
faq.answer: Yes, on a file system: [Amazon Elastic File System (EFS)] (fargate-faq-efs-for-persistent-storage) gives persistent storage.
faq.quote: Amazon Elastic File System (EFS) an be used to provide persistent storage to workloads running on AWS Fargate.
faq.quote_note: Copy the AWS sentence exactly, typo 'an' included.

faq.question: Is Amazon ECR a global service?
faq.answer: No. ECR is a [Regional service] (ecr-faq-regional-service); replicate images to the other Regions.
faq.quote: Amazon ECR is a Regional service and is designed to give you flexibility in how images are deployed.

faq.question: Can ECS Anywhere run in an air-gapped data center?
faq.answer: No. The servers need a [stable internet connection] (ecs-anywhere-faq-needs-stable-internet-not-air-gapped) to the ECS control plane.
faq.quote: Hence, it requires your on-premises compute to have a stable internet connection to communicate with the in-region ECS control plane.

faq.question: Can a team keep its Kubernetes tools when it moves to Amazon EKS?
faq.answer: Yes. Applications are compatible with [any standard Kubernetes environment] (eks-faq-runs-open-source-kubernetes-compatible).
faq.quote: Amazon EKS runs the open-source Kubernetes software, so you can use all the existing plug-ins and tooling from the Kubernetes community.

question_slots.plan: Context: a company moved a monolithic application into containers on Amazon ECS with AWS Fargate. Changed phrase (the only difference from q005): 'The application code in the container must read objects from an S3 bucket.' Ask with a least-privilege qualifier ('Which solution meets this requirement and follows the principle of least privilege?'). Options identical in q001 and q005, written in neutral words: (a) add the needed permissions to the task role of the task definition [key here]; (b) add the needed permissions to the task execution role of the task definition [trap containers-trap-execution-role-for-app; key in q005]; (c) attach an instance profile with the needed permissions to the Fargate tasks [impossible-feature: ecs-task-role-fargate-no-instance-profile]; (d) store an access key with the needed permissions as an environment variable in the task definition [iam-trap-keys-on-instance, violates-qualifier]. Facts: ecs-task-role-gives-app-code-aws-permissions, ecs-task-execution-role-for-agents, ecs-task-role-fargate-no-instance-profile, ecs-iam-role-table-task-role.

A containerized job processes recorded calls. It starts at sporadic times when a customer asks for a bulk export, and each run takes 2 to 3 hours. The company wants no servers to manage. LEAST operational overhead. Key: run the job as an Amazon ECS task on AWS Fargate (fargate-guide-containers-run-indefinitely-no-hard-limit, fargate-no-provision-vm-clusters). Distractors: a Lambda function from a container image with the timeout raised through Service Quotas [lambda-trap-timeout-raisable; impossible-feature with lambda-timeout-max or lambda-fargate-no-execution-time-limit]; an EC2 instance that runs all day with a cron job [violates-qualifier]; an EKS cluster with a managed node group that runs the job as a pod [violates-qualifier; ec2-trap-lambda-runs-any-job not needed]. Do not key on how the task is started; the stem can say 'an application already calls RunTask' or leave the trigger out.

An ECS service on Fargate must keep at a minimum two tasks running at all times; the other tasks can tolerate interruption. MOST cost-effective. Key: a capacity provider strategy with a base of 2 on FARGATE and the larger weight on FARGATE_SPOT (ecs-capacity-provider-manages-infrastructure-scaling, fargate-spot-no-on-demand-replacement, fargate-faq-spot-up-to-70-percent-discount). Distractors: FARGATE_SPOT only, with a minimum task count of 2 in service auto scaling [containers-trap-fargate-spot-falls-back]; FARGATE only with a Compute Savings Plan [violates-qualifier]; EC2 Spot Instances in an Auto Scaling group capacity provider with a base of 2 [wrong-configuration: Spot Instances can be interrupted too; ec2-trap-spot-for-uninterruptible]. Do not key on the weight arithmetic.

Context shared with q010: a company runs 20 tasks of a data processing service on Amazon ECS with AWS Fargate and does not want to manage instances. Changed phrase: 'The tasks process intermittent batch work and can be stopped and restarted at any time without harm.' MOST cost-effective. Options identical in q004 and q010: (a) run the tasks with the FARGATE_SPOT capacity provider [key here]; (b) buy a Compute Savings Plan for the Fargate usage [key in q010; here violates-qualifier: a commitment for an intermittent load; ec2-spot-vs-savings-plans-guideline]; (c) buy an EC2 Instance Savings Plan for the instance family that Fargate uses [misconception: it applies to a specific instance family; ec2-savings-plans-two-ec2-types-flexibility, fargate-compute-savings-plans-cover-fargate-lambda]; (d) move the tasks to EC2 Spot Instances in an Auto Scaling group capacity provider [violates the 'no instances to manage' constraint]. Facts: fargate-faq-spot-up-to-70-percent-discount, fargate-spot-interruption-tolerant-discount, ec2-spot-vs-savings-plans-guideline.

Same context and same four options as q001. Changed phrase: 'New tasks stop before the container starts, because they cannot pull the image from a private Amazon ECR repository.' Key moves to (b) the task execution role (ecs-task-execution-role-use-cases, ecr-ecs-agent-pull-permissions). Option (a), the task role, now carries the misconception 'the task role is used to pull the image' with fact ecs-task-execution-role-for-agents. The twin line of each question quotes the changed phrase of the other.

A company migrates its containerized applications to Amazon ECS. The applications use public base images from Docker Hub. The tasks must pull the images from Amazon ECR, and the images in ECR must stay current with the upstream registry; a one-time copy does not meet this. Key: an ECR pull through cache rule for Docker Hub, with the credentials in a Secrets Manager secret (ecr-pull-through-cache-keeps-cache-current, ecr-pull-through-cache-upstream-registries-auth). Distractors: copy each image once into a private repository [misconception: newer versions are not pulled automatically; ecr-migrate-one-time-copy-no-auto-update]; an ECR replication rule with Docker Hub as the source [sibling-confusion: replication copies between ECR registries; ecr-replication-cross-region-cross-account]; pull directly from Docker Hub through a NAT gateway [different-problem: the requirement is ECR]. Difficulty 1: qualifier none is allowed.

(Select TWO.) An ECS service runs Fargate tasks in private subnets. Stringent security rules forbid any route to the internet. An internal Application Load Balancer sends requests to the tasks, and the tasks pull their image from Amazon ECR. Which combination of steps meets these requirements? Keys: (1) interface VPC endpoints for the ECR API and the Docker registry plus a gateway endpoint for Amazon S3 (ecr-vpc-endpoints-fargate-need-ecr-and-s3); (2) a target group with the ip target type (fargate-target-group-ip-target-type). Distractors: a target group with the instance target type [containers-trap-instance-target-type]; public IP addresses on the tasks and a route to an internet gateway [violates the no-internet rule; vpc-trap-public-ip-is-enough]; a NAT gateway for the private subnets [violates the no-internet rule]. Five options.

A company runs all its Kubernetes pods on Amazon EKS with AWS Fargate. A new rule needs a log agent next to every application container. The company wants to keep all pods on Fargate. LEAST operational overhead. Key: run the agent as a sidecar container in each pod (eks-fargate-no-daemonsets). Distractors: deploy the agent as a DaemonSet [containers-trap-fargate-runs-anything; impossible-feature with eks-fargate-no-daemonsets]; add a managed node group and run the DaemonSet there [violates the 'keep all pods on Fargate' constraint]; add the agent to the Fargate profile [keyword-bait: a profile only selects pods, eks-fargate-profile-selects-pods].

question_slots.plan: A company runs its applications on a self-managed Kubernetes cluster in its data center, with Kubernetes manifests and kubectl. It moves to AWS with minimal code changes, does not want to refactor, and does not want to operate the Kubernetes control plane. LEAST operational overhead. Key: an Amazon EKS cluster with managed node groups, deploying the existing manifests (eks-whitepaper-natural-migration-path-for-kubernetes, eks-faq-migrate-standard-kubernetes-without-code-changes, eks-faq-managed-kubernetes-no-control-plane-to-run). Distractors: rewrite the manifests as ECS task definitions on Fargate [violates 'minimal code changes'; how-the-exam-asks-trap-works-means-correct]; install Kubernetes on EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group [violates-qualifier: you run the control plane]; install EKS Anywhere on EC2 instances in a VPC [impossible-feature: eks-anywhere-faq-not-supported-on-aws-cloud]. Never key on EKS Auto Mode (volatile).

Same context and same four options as q004. Changed phrase: 'The tasks serve a steady-state load all day, every day, and must not be interrupted.' Key moves to (b) the Compute Savings Plan (fargate-compute-savings-plans-cover-fargate-lambda, ec2-spot-vs-savings-plans-guideline). Option (a), FARGATE_SPOT, now carries ec2-trap-spot-for-uninterruptible (fargate-spot-two-minute-interruption-warning). The twin line of each question quotes the changed phrase of the other.

A service on Amazon ECS with AWS Fargate runs tasks across Availability Zones. All tasks must read and write the same files, and the files must stay durable when tasks are replaced. Key: an Amazon EFS file system mounted as a volume by every task (ecs-efs-volumes-shared-persistent-across-instances, fargate-faq-efs-for-persistent-storage). Distractors: raise the ephemeral storage of each task to the maximum [containers-trap-task-storage-persists; fargate-faq-ephemeral-storage-20-gib-erased]; attach an Amazon EBS volume to each task [misconception: one new volume per task, deleted with a service task; ecs-ebs-volume-one-per-task-new-volume, ecs-ebs-volume-service-task-deleted-on-termination]; a bind mount shared by the containers of the task [different-problem: shared only inside one task; fargate-task-containers-share-resources]. Difficulty 1; qualifier none is allowed.

(Select TWO.) An ECS service runs on EC2 instances of an Auto Scaling group. Service auto scaling lowers the task count at night, but the number of instances stays the same, and most instances run few tasks. The group has sufficient instances for the day peak. Which combination of steps reduces cost the MOST? Keys: (1) an Auto Scaling group capacity provider with managed scaling turned on (ecs-cluster-auto-scaling-managed-scaling-asg-capacity-provider, ecs-cluster-auto-scaling-reservation-above-or-below-target); (2) the binpack placement strategy on memory or CPU (ecs-placement-binpack-least-unused-cpu-memory). Distractors: lower the minimum task count of the service auto scaling policy [containers-trap-service-scaling-adds-instances]; the spread placement strategy on instance ID [wrong-configuration: ecs-placement-strategy-types-binpack-random-spread]; a target tracking policy on average CPU attached directly to the Auto Scaling group [misconception: ECS creates and manages that policy for cluster auto scaling; ecs-cluster-auto-scaling-policy-managed-by-ecs; auto-scaling-trap-ec2-auto-scaling-for-any-resource only if the text states that belief]. Five options.

tasks.title: Read the Fargate quotas of your account
tasks.kills: "Fargate is serverless, so no account quota limits how many tasks run."
tasks.plan: In AWS CloudShell, read-only, $0. Step 1: list the Fargate quotas of the current Region (aws service-quotas list-service-quotas --service-code fargate, with a --query that prints name, value and adjustable). Expect the On-Demand and Spot vCPU quotas: the default is [6 vCPUs] (fargate-ondemand-vcpu-quota, fargate-spot-vcpu-quota), quotas count the [number of vCPU cores used] (fargate-faq-quotas-based-on-vcpu-per-region-account), and a new account can show lower values that you can [raise these soft limits] for (fargate-faq-new-accounts-lower-quotas-raisable). Step 2: the same command with --region us-west-2 (expect a separate value for that Region). Creates nothing. Confirm the command and service code with tasks check-cli --reference; if fargate is not a valid service code, park the task and report it.

tasks.title: Create an ECR repository with immutable tags and look for it in another Region
tasks.kills: "One ECR repository serves tasks in every Region."
tasks.plan: In AWS CloudShell, about 10 minutes, $0 (an empty repository stores no data; you pay for [the amount of data you store], ecr-faq-pricing-storage-and-internet-transfer). Step 1: aws ecr create-repository --repository-name saa-containers-t02 --image-tag-mutability IMMUTABLE --image-scanning-configuration scanOnPush=true --tags Key=book,Value=saa Key=task,Value=containers-t02 (us-east-1). Step 2: aws ecr describe-repositories --repository-names saa-containers-t02 (expect imageTagMutability IMMUTABLE, scanOnPush true, and encryptionType AES256: the default is [server-side encryption with Amazon S3-managed encryption keys], ecr-encryption-default-sse-s3-aes256). Step 3, break it: predict whether the repository exists in us-west-2; run the same describe command with --region us-west-2; expect RepositoryNotFoundException; explain: ECR is a [Regional service] (ecr-faq-regional-service). Cleanup: aws ecr delete-repository --repository-name saa-containers-t02. Verify by name (TOOLS-rules R6, T108): aws ecr describe-repositories --repository-names saa-containers-t02, expect RepositoryNotFoundException. Commands from the ECR CLI reference pages in the corpus (tasks check-cli --reference).

tasks.kills: "A Fargate task can use any network mode, as a task on an EC2 instance can."
tasks.status: optional: write it only if the commands can be grounded in a CLI reference page of the corpus; the template needs at least 1 Try, which containers-t02 covers
tasks.plan: In AWS CloudShell, about 10 minutes, $0 (a registered task definition runs nothing). Step 1, break it: predict, then aws ecs register-task-definition --family saa-containers-t03 --requires-compatibilities FARGATE --network-mode bridge --cpu 256 --memory 512 with one small public container definition and --tags key=book,value=saa key=task,value=containers-t03 (the ECS tag syntax is lowercase key/value: check it); expect a ClientException that names the network mode; explain: Fargate tasks [require the `awsvpc` network mode] (fargate-requires-awsvpc-network-mode). Step 2, the fix: the same command with --network-mode awsvpc; expect a task definition with revision 1. Cleanup: aws ecs deregister-task-definition --task-definition saa-containers-t03:1, then aws ecs delete-task-definitions --task-definitions saa-containers-t03:1. Verify by name: aws ecs describe-task-definition --task-definition saa-containers-t03:1, expect status DELETE_IN_PROGRESS or a ClientException; if no fact or reference page supports the expected result after deletion, park the task.

speak.prompt: ECS or EKS? My one Kubernetes engineer says that EKS is the standard.

plan.ten_second: Both run your containers, and both work with Fargate. EKS fits teams that already run Kubernetes; ECS is less to operate for you.
key_points_must: Both orchestrate containers and both run on Fargate (fargate-whitepaper-own-kernel-for-ecs-and-eks).
EKS runs upstream Kubernetes, so existing manifests and tools work (eks-faq-runs-open-source-kubernetes-compatible).
EKS has a per cluster per hour fee; ECS has no additional charge (eks-pricing-per-cluster-per-hour-fee, ecs-faq-no-additional-charge).
Skills decide: Kubernetes needs a team that handles frequent cluster upgrades (eks-decision-guide-kubernetes-skills-sre-teams).
key_points_nice: A Kubernetes version gets 14 months of standard support, then extended support at extra cost (eks-standard-support-14-months, eks-pricing-extended-support-additional-cost-per-cluster-hour).
must_not_say: error: 'ECS is not for production; EKS is the standard on AWS.' correct: ECS is a fully managed container orchestration service (ecs-fully-managed-orchestration).
error: 'With EKS we would run the Kubernetes control plane ourselves.' correct: EKS manages the control plane for you (eks-managed-control-plane-across-azs).
follow_ups: Can we move from ECS to EKS later? Yes: the same images in Amazon ECR work with both (ecr-faq-integrated-with-ecs-eks-lambda); only the task definitions become Kubernetes manifests.
Does Fargate Spot work with EKS? No: Amazon EKS does not support Fargate Spot (eks-fargate-no-spot); EKS uses Spot Instances in node groups.
plan.in_your_case: One Kubernetes engineer and six services: ECS on Fargate. Check-back question: 'Who would handle the cluster upgrades if your Kubernetes engineer is away?'

speak.persona: a startup founder in office hours
speak.prompt: Should we run our containers on Fargate or on EC2 instances? We want low cost and little operations work.

plan.ten_second: Start on Fargate: no instances to patch, and you pay per second for what each task asks for. Move to EC2 for GPUs or large steady fleets.
key_points_must: Fargate removes instance provisioning and scaling (fargate-no-provision-vm-clusters).
Fargate bills the requested vCPU and memory per second (ecs-faq-fargate-billing-granularity).
EC2 capacity fits control, GPUs and large price-optimized workloads (ecs-ec2-capacity-large-workloads-price-optimized, fargate-faq-gpu-not-supported).
Fargate Spot and Compute Savings Plans lower the Fargate bill (fargate-faq-spot-up-to-70-percent-discount, fargate-compute-savings-plans-cover-fargate-lambda).
must_not_say: error: 'Fargate always costs more than EC2.' correct: no AWS page says so; on Fargate you pay for what you provision (fargate-guide-pricing-per-second-pay-for-what-you-provision).
error: 'Fargate can run GPU work too.' correct: GPU workloads are not supported on Fargate today (fargate-faq-gpu-not-supported).
follow_ups: What happens when a Fargate Spot task is stopped? It gets a two-minute warning as SIGTERM, and the container must save its work (fargate-spot-warning-delivery-sigterm-eventbridge, fargate-spot-container-must-handle-sigterm).

Does a Savings Plan cover Fargate? Compute Savings Plans do (fargate-compute-savings-plans-cover-fargate-lambda); EC2 Instance Savings Plans apply to an instance family (ec2-savings-plans-two-ec2-types-flexibility).
plan.in_your_case: Check-back question: 'Do any of your containers need a GPU or access to the host?'

cards.front: In AWS Lambda, the longest run of one invocation is {{c1::15 minutes per invocation}}; Fargate has no such limit.
On Fargate Spot, before AWS stops a task, the task gets a {{c1::two-minute warning}}.
Fargate Spot runs interruption-tolerant ECS tasks at {{c1::up to a 70 percent discount}} off the Fargate price.
In AWS Fargate, a Linux task is billed {{c1::per second with a 1-minute minimum}}.
In AWS Fargate, an ECS task gets {{c1::20 GiB}} of ephemeral storage by default, erased when it stops.
In Amazon ECS, task role or task execution role: which one does the application code use to call Amazon S3?
cards.extra: The task execution role is for the ECS container and Fargate agents: pulling images, sending logs, reading secrets.

cards.front: In AWS Fargate, can a task run a privileged container?
cards.extra: Privileged containers or access are currently unavailable on Fargate; use EC2 capacity or ECS Managed Instances.

cards.front: Kubernetes clusters in a data center with no connection to AWS, supported by AWS: which service?
cards.extra: EKS Hybrid Nodes and ECS Anywhere need a connection to the AWS Region.

cards.front: In an ECS service on Fargate, can the load balancer target group use the target type instance?
cards.back: No: use the ip target type
cards.extra: Tasks in awsvpc mode are associated with a network interface, not an EC2 instance.

cards.front: An ECS service on Fargate Spot must always keep two tasks running: what do you set?
cards.back: A base of 2 on the FARGATE capacity provider
cards.extra: Fargate does not replace Spot capacity with on-demand capacity.

cards.front: In Amazon ECS, service auto scaling or cluster auto scaling: which one adds EC2 instances?
cards.back: Cluster auto scaling (managed scaling of a capacity provider)
cards.extra: Service auto scaling changes only the desired number of tasks.

cards.front: In Amazon ECR, can one repository serve tasks in every Region without extra cost?
cards.back: No: ECR is Regional; replicate the images
cards.extra: A pull from another Region adds latency and data transfer costs.

diagrams.title: One request through an ECS service on Fargate
diagrams.claim: An ECS service runs tasks from an ECR image on Fargate, and the load balancer sends each request to one task.
diagrams.alt: A VPC with private subnets in two Availability Zones. An Application Load Balancer sends requests to the Fargate tasks of one ECS service. The tasks pull their image from Amazon ECR and write to Amazon S3.
say: The ECS service starts tasks on Fargate, and Fargate will try its best to spread tasks across Availability Zones.
The task execution role grants the Amazon ECS container and Fargate agents permission to pull the image from Amazon ECR.
The awsvpc mode provides each task with an elastic network interface, and the load balancer sends each request to one task.
The task role lets the application use other AWS services, such as Amazon S3.
diagrams.note: Size s. Nodes: users (left), Application Load Balancer (elb icon), two Fargate tasks in two private subnets in AZ 1 and AZ 2 inside one VPC group, Amazon ECR (ecr icon) above compute, Amazon S3 (s3 icon) on the right; numbered steps 1 to 4 on the edges in the order of 'say'. In the Markdown steps link step 1 [try its best to spread tasks] (fargate-no-placement-strategies-best-effort-az-spread), step 2 [grants the Amazon ECS container and Fargate agents] (ecs-task-execution-role-for-agents), step 3 [provides each task with an elastic network interface] (fargate-requires-awsvpc-network-mode), step 4 [use other AWS services] (ecs-iam-role-table-task-role); rephrase a step only so that the verbatim display fits, and keep spec say and Markdown steps equal (L703).
